name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,128

blocks.note: first meaning: crooked, dishonest, on the wrong side of the law
second meaning: a natural inclination or knack

explanation.surface: A psychologist's phrase for someone drawn to wrongdoing.
explanation.walkthrough: The two words look like adjective and noun of one phrase, but each is a separate meaning; 'bent' for crooked is informal British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as slang for dishonest or corrupt and also as a noun meaning a natural leaning or aptitude.

indicators.note: something disseminated is scattered widely, so the letters before it are spread about into a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these three words, taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone complains that a man has been spreading rubbish about them.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyewash is an informal word for talk meant to deceive or impress, that is, rubbish or claptrap.

clue.text: Central idea in article on this writer

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece sitting on another is placed above it, so the first part comes before the second

blocks.note: the definite article
the setter referring to themself

explanation.surface: A literary critic identifies the main point of an essay about its own author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the usual crossword way for a setter to say ME.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the subject or main thread running through a work, its core notion.

indicators.note: one item placed in another means it goes inside that second word
spread suggests the letters are scattered about and laid out again in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A performer in a nightclub show passes on germs to the audience.
explanation.walkthrough: The I can go anywhere in CABARET, since the whole lot is then mixed.
explanation.definitionFit: Bugs is an informal term for germs, and bacteria are the microbes that commonly cause infections.

blocks.note: first meaning: a flying mammal, of which the vampire is one species
second meaning: the wooden implement a batsman uses in cricket

explanation.surface: A spooky question about whether a bloodsucker has joined the local sports team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cricket club' reads like a society of players, but it is the implement used to hit the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: The vampire is an example of a winged night mammal, and a cricketer strikes the ball with a flat wooden paddle of the same name.

clue.text: Portions from fishmonger in old pouches

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: chunks of a common white fish sold at the counter
second meaning: the flaps worn over the crotch on men's breeches in past centuries

explanation.surface: Cuts of fish from the shop are wrapped in ancient bags.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as COD PIECES to get the fishmonger's portions; joined, it is the Tudor garment.
explanation.definitionFit: A codpiece was a bag or flap attached to the front of men's hose in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

clue.text: Forming a unit, see unit formed

indicators.note: formed means shaped or made up, so the preceding letters are moulded into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A sentence that echoes itself, about pieces being assembled into a single whole.
explanation.definitionFit: En suite is French for 'in sequence', describing rooms that join together as one set, such as a bedroom with its own bathroom.

clue.text: I may be represented by this Asian country!

blocks.clueFragment: I may be represented by this
blocks.note: first meaning: the code word radio operators use for the ninth letter
second meaning: the large nation of South Asia

explanation.surface: A patriot declares that their homeland could stand for them personally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I' reads as a speaker, but it is the letter, which the NATO phonetic alphabet spells out with this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is the name of the populous republic on the South Asian subcontinent.

indicators.note: involving means including or taking in, so the first word wraps round the second

blocks.note: an act is a deed
to tax someone is to strain or try them, to test them

explanation.surface: A complaint about an unpopular piece of tax legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Act' and 'tax' suggest a parliamentary bill, but act is a deed and tax is a verb meaning to strain.
explanation.definitionFit: To detest is to loathe intensely, so something hated is something detested.

blocks.note: first meaning: secondary or minor
second meaning: the edge or slope of something, as of a river or hill

explanation.surface: Sounds like a financial institution owned by a parent company.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pairs the words as corporate finance, but they are two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Used as an adjective it means secondary or lesser; as a noun it is a flank or slope, like a riverbank.

indicators.note: something seen in a phrase is visible inside its letters, running across the word break

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A Nordic visitor is spotted at a headland in Shetland.
explanation.walkthrough: Skelda Ness is a real headland in Shetland, which has strong Norse roots.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Denmark is one of the Nordic peoples of northern Europe.

clue.text: Racism — it is brandished as a weapon

indicators.note: brandished means waved about, so the letters are flourished into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A statement that bigotry gets wielded to hurt people.
explanation.definitionFit: A scimitar is a curved single-edged sword of Middle Eastern origin, an arm for fighting.

indicators.note: surprisingly hints the letters turn out in an unexpected order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A march by the Scottish National Party goes off without a hitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The SNP is the Scottish National Party; 'smooth' is a verb here, not an adjective for the parade.
explanation.definitionFit: To sandpaper is to rub a surface with abrasive paper to make it even and polished.

indicators.note: one thing in another sits inside it, so the first word goes within the second

blocks.note: Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
a hake is a sea fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A tinned sardine has been knocked over.
explanation.walkthrough: Tin is the metal, whose chemical symbol is from Latin stannum.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone shaken has been disturbed or rattled emotionally, which is to be distressed.

blocks.note: to keep a rule or custom is to respect or observe it
the British informal word for mother

explanation.surface: Advice to a child: honour your mother and don't answer back.
explanation.walkthrough: Mum is British for mom.
explanation.definitionFit: Keep mum is an idiom meaning say nothing and keep a secret quiet.

clue.text: Arrest that woman, said Roman leader?

indicators.note: said means spoken out loud, so we want words that sound like the phrase

blocks.note: to arrest is to seize, and that woman is her

explanation.surface: An order shouted in ancient Rome, perhaps at Cleopatra.
explanation.definitionFit: Julius Caesar was the dictator of the Roman Republic, and later emperors took his name as a title.

indicators.note: recalled suggests being called back, so the word is taken back the other way

blocks.note: ca is the abbreviation of circa, Latin for about
a count is a nobleman in continental Europe

explanation.surface: A tale remembered about an aristocrat from the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recalled about' looks like 'remembered concerning', but it is the reversed abbreviation for circa.
explanation.definitionFit: An account is a narrative or report of events, a tale.

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the word is kept

blocks.note: the second and fourth letters
to lure is to tempt

explanation.surface: An angler has a go at fishing by putting out bait and lures.
explanation.walkthrough: Bait and lures sound like fishing gear, but bait supplies only its even letters and lures is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, tries means makes an effort, which is what someone who attempts does.

clue.text: I’m going to accept international crown

indicators.note: to accept is to take in, so the first expression holds the second inside it

blocks.note: ta-ra is an informal British goodbye, said when leaving
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A monarch announcing departure to receive a crown from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Ta-ra is a northern English way of saying goodbye; 'I'm going' stands for that farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiara is a jewelled ornamental headdress like a small crown, worn by women on formal occasions.

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
ace is slang for excellent

explanation.surface: A woman described as having striking looks.
explanation.definitionFit: Features can mean the whole set of eyes, nose and mouth, collectively the visage.

indicators.note: to swallow something is to take it inside, so the first word goes round the second

blocks.note: Fr is the abbreviation for Father, a priest's title
the emu is a big flightless Australian bird

explanation.surface: A priest gulping down a large bird, bones and all.
explanation.definitionFit: The femur is the thigh bone, the longest in the human skeleton.

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only the final letter is taken

blocks.note: hostilities are open fighting, a war
the final letter

explanation.surface: Fierce fighting near Actium, site of the sea battle where Octavian beat Antony and Cleopatra.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' looks like 'near', but it means the end letter of the place name.
explanation.definitionFit: Heated in the sense of having been raised in temperature is moderately hot, as in warmed water.

clue.text: Men almost in truck shot in the arm

indicators.note: almost means nearly all, so the last letter of the word is dropped
one item in another goes inside it, so the shortened word sits within the vehicle

blocks.note: a pickup is a light open-backed truck
taken as written

explanation.surface: A few men nearly hitched a ride in a lorry and got a boost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shot in the arm' suggests an injection, but it is the idiom for a boost.
explanation.definitionFit: A pick-me-up is a tonic or stimulant that restores energy, which is what the idiom for a revitalising boost means.

clue.text: Knave of clubs put on notice

indicators.note: in a down entry, the first piece is put on top of the second, so it comes first

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
an ad, or advertisement, is a public notice

explanation.surface: The jack of clubs is placed on display, as in a card game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knave of clubs' looks like a playing card, but knave is the definition and clubs just a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Knave is an old word for a dishonest rogue, and a cad is a man who behaves dishonourably.

clue.text: Very drunk actor with case of Moselle wine

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so just the outer letters of the word are kept

blocks.note: a ham is an overacting performer
first and last letters
red is a type of wine

explanation.surface: A performer who got legless on a crate of German white.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of Moselle' suggests a dozen bottles, but it means the word's outer letters; Moselle is a German wine region.
explanation.definitionFit: Hammered is slang for extremely intoxicated, like plastered or smashed.

blocks.note: first meaning: the famous grand hotel on Piccadilly, a street in central London
second meaning: a brand of buttery savoury biscuit sold in North America

explanation.walkthrough: 'A cracker' is British slang for something excellent, praising the hotel, but here it names the snack brand.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ritz is the famous London hotel, and Ritz is also the name of a popular round snack biscuit.
